traveler: Ahmad al-Qalqashandi (Shihab al-Din Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn Ali ibn Ahmad al-Fazari al-Shafi'i al-Qalqashandi)
title: The Dawn of the Blind: a Delta Village, the Scribe of the Scroll, and the Cipher Chapter That Outlived the Mamluks
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Baghdad, the treatise on drawing out the hidden
stops.date_confidence: ninth century; c. 850 is a conventional midpoint of al-Kindi's working life, not a dated event
stops.campa: Abu Yusuf Ya'qub al-Kindi writes a treatise on drawing out the hidden, Risala fi Istikhraj al-Mu'amma. Its method is counting. Every language leans on some letters more than others, and a cipher that hides the letter cannot hide the leaning, so the frequencies of the enciphered page are set beside the frequencies of ordinary speech until the disguise gives way. It is the earliest systematic description of the technique that anyone has found. Five centuries later, in a fortress above Cairo, a Mamluk secretary will copy its descendants into a manual for clerks.
suggested_refs: Al-Kindi, Risala fi Istikhraj al-Mu'amma, the earliest known systematic description of frequency analysis

stops.name: Cairo, Ibn Adlan and the ninety characters
stops.date_confidence: death attested at 666 AH / 1268 CE; the treatise for al-Ashraf Musa is undated within his lifetime
stops.campa: Ibn Adlan, born at Mosul, teaches Arabic for more than two decades at the Salihiyya mosque in Cairo and writes on the solving of ciphers for the Ayyubid ruler al-Ashraf Musa. His addition to al-Kindi's method is a threshold. Frequency analysis needs text to work on, and he fixes the minimum at ninety characters: below that the sample is too small, the letters in it do not yet behave like the language they came from, and the counting lies. He dies in Cairo in 666 of the Hijra, 1268 by the Christian reckoning.
suggested_refs: Ibn Adlan's treatise on cryptanalysis, dedicated to the Ayyubid al-Ashraf Musa

stops.name: Cairo, the treasures key of Ibn al-Durayhim
stops.date_confidence: c. 1350 per Muslim Heritage; the treatise carries no firm date and the figure is approximate
stops.campa: Ali ibn Muhammad ibn al-Durayhim al-Mawsili sets down eight cipher systems in a book called Miftah al-Kunuz fi Idah al-Marmuz, the Treasures Key for the Clarifying of the Enciphered. He works in the same Cairo whose chancery drafts the sultan's secret correspondence, and a reputation follows him through its quarter: that he reads enciphered letters aloud on sight, and the old picture-writing on the Egyptian monuments as well. That last is a tradition no document supports. The book is attested, and it carries his name.
stops.quote: Almost all of these references were based on a manuscript by Ali ibn ad-Durayhim written around 1350 CE, titled Muftah Al-Kunuz fi Idhah Al-Marmuz (The Treasures Key in Deciphering Cryptograms)
suggested_refs: Ibn al-Durayhim, Miftah al-Kunuz fi Idah al-Marmuz, the eight cipher systems

stops.name: Cairo, the year the cipher master dies
stops.date_confidence: 762 AH / 1361 per Arabic Wikipedia; English Wikipedia gives the range 1359-1362. No source consulted names his place of death; this pin is the chancery milieu, not an attested location
stops.campa: Ibn al-Durayhim dies in 762 of the Hijra. English sources spread the year across 1359 to 1362, and no source consulted names the town he dies in; the nisba al-Mawsili records only where he was born. Somewhere in the Mamluk lands the man who classified the eight cipher systems stops writing. In a Delta village northeast of Cairo the boy who will quote him is five or six years old, learning his letters in the ordinary way. Who buried Ibn al-Durayhim, and where, no source consulted says.
suggested_refs: The disputed death date of Ibn al-Durayhim, 762 AH, and the silence of the sources on its place

segments.name: The Village That Gave Him His Name

stops.name: Qalqashanda, a son born in the eastern Delta
stops.date_confidence: 756 AH; the year is attested and the month and day are not recorded. English sources give 1355 or 1356. Coordinates approximate: no mapping database consulted returns the village
stops.campa: In 756 of the Hijra a son is born to Ali ibn Ahmad in the village of Qalqashanda, in the province of Qalyubiyya, among the canals and the black soil of the eastern Delta. They name him Ahmad, and the honorific that will travel with the name, Shihab al-Din, means flame of the faith. No mapping database consulted returns the village, though the family living in it kept a written pedigree. Of the household nothing else survives: no property, no father's trade, no anecdote of the boy.
suggested_refs: The village of Qalqashanda in Qalyubiyya, source of the nisba al-Qalqashandi

stops.name: Qalqashanda, the Fazara line and the whole name
stops.date_confidence: the descent is reported by Arabic Wikipedia and repeated in the English and Marefa entries; no genealogical document is cited by any of them
stops.campa: The family traces itself to the Fazara, an Arab tribe of the Ghatafan confederation, and the full name he will one day sign carries the whole apparatus: Shihab al-Din Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn Ali ibn Ahmad al-Fazari al-Shafi'i al-Qalqashandi. Tribe, legal school, and village, in that order, before the man himself. He will write two books on the genealogy of the Arabs, one of them on the tribes of his own century. No genealogical document behind the Fazara claim is cited by any source that repeats it.
suggested_refs: The Fazara of the Ghatafan confederation, claimed ancestry of the Qalqashandi family

stops.name: Qalyub, the district town on the maps
stops.date_confidence: Qalyub coordinates per English Wikipedia; used as the nearest mapped proxy for a village whose own position is not confirmed
stops.campa: The district town of Qalyub stands a short ride from the village, the nearest place any map will fix, and the modern references cannot agree where the village sits with respect to it. One account puts the birthplace at 30.18 north and 31.23 east; another places it two and a half kilometres away and calls the figure a stand-in for Qalyub, which lies further north again. The disagreement is trivial on the ground and total on paper. On the ground it is a few minutes' walk between the three of them. The province is not in doubt.
suggested_refs: Qalyub, Qalyubiyya governorate, nearest mapped settlement to Qalqashanda

segments.name: The Schools of Cairo and Alexandria

stops.name: Al-Azhar, Cairo: the expected classroom
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No source consulted places him at al-Azhar, and no source dates his schooling; the plausible span is the 1360s to the 1380s
stops.campa: He is sent to Cairo for the sciences: Arabic letters, rhetoric, and the jurisprudence of the Shafi'i school, the training that makes a man employable in a chancery. Al-Azhar is the great Shafi'i house of the Mamluk capital, and it is where a student of his kind would be expected to sit. No source consulted puts him inside it, or inside any other named college in the city. What the biographers hand down is the list of subjects: not the buildings, not the teachers, not the years.
suggested_refs: Al-Azhar Mosque, principal centre of Shafi'i learning in Mamluk Cairo
sources: General knowledge of Mamluk Cairo educational geography; not confirmed for al-Qalqashandi in any source consulted

stops.name: Alexandria, the great shaykhs of the age
stops.date_confidence: single-source and undated. Arabic Wikipedia alone reports study at Alexandria; the date here is a marker inside the c. 1360s-1380s span, not evidence
stops.campa: His biographers say he studied at Cairo and at Alexandria, under the great shaykhs of the age. The phrase is all there is. No Alexandrian teacher is named, no institution, no year, and a single Arabic account carries the claim with nothing corroborating it. Alexandria in these years is a working port with its own colleges and its own Shafi'i jurists, three days from the capital by river and road. Whether he ever went down the western branch of the Nile to reach it is the one question about his movements that the sources raise and then drop.
stops.quote: the great shaykhs of the age
stops.quote_source: Arabic Wikipedia, 'al-Qalqashandi', the biographers' phrase for his teachers
suggested_refs: The unnamed Alexandrian teachers of al-Qalqashandi, an uncorroborated report

stops.name: Bayn al-Qasrayn, the madrasa of al-Salih Najm al-Din Ayyub
stops.date_confidence: the teaching post is attested before Ibn al-Mulaqqin's death in 804 AH / 1401 CE; that al-Qalqashandi attended this venue is not attested at all
stops.campa: On the processional street of Bayn al-Qasrayn, opposite the Qalawun complex, stands the madrasa and mausoleum of the last Ayyubid sultan al-Salih Najm al-Din Ayyub, built between 1242 and 1249, the tomb chamber added by Shajar al-Durr. Here the jurist Ibn al-Mulaqqin holds a professorship in Shafi'i law. Arabic sources make al-Qalqashandi his student. The English account of Ibn al-Mulaqqin lists eight notable students, among them Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani and al-Maqrizi. Al-Qalqashandi is not one of them, and neither list was built to be exhaustive.
suggested_refs: The Salihiyya madrasa on al-Mu'izz street, where Ibn al-Mulaqqin taught Shafi'i fiqh
sources: Wikipedia, 'Madrasa of al-Salih Najm al-Din Ayyub'

stops.name: The mosque of al-Hakim, a possible classroom
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Ibn al-Mulaqqin's preaching post here is attested; no source links al-Qalqashandi to the building
stops.campa: Ibn al-Mulaqqin preaches at the mosque of al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah beside Bab al-Futuh at the northern wall, a Fatimid congregational building already four centuries old when he mounts its pulpit. It stands a short walk north of the madrasa where he lectures on Shafi'i law, up the same processional street. The pin here marks a possibility rather than a record. A student attached to a teacher follows him between his posts, and this is one of the places the teaching happened; whether al-Qalqashandi ever stood in this courtyard is recorded nowhere at all.
suggested_refs: The mosque of al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah, one of Ibn al-Mulaqqin's teaching and preaching posts

stops.name: Dar al-Hadith al-Kamiliyya, the shape of the curriculum
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the coordinates are approximate and the madrasa's exact site is not independently verified in the sources consulted
stops.campa: For a season Ibn al-Mulaqqin lectures on hadith at the Dar al-Hadith of the Kamiliyya madrasa, an Ayyubid foundation for the science of prophetic tradition. Al-Qalqashandi's own training in hadith is nowhere described. What the record does hold is the shape of the curriculum a man of his generation passes through: Qur'an, grammar, rhetoric, Shafi'i fiqh, and the formulae of composition. Only the last of those is a trade, and it is the one that will pay him. The exact site of the Kamiliyya is not independently verified in the sources consulted, and these coordinates are approximate.
suggested_refs: The Dar al-Hadith of the Kamiliyya madrasa, Cairo

segments.name: Katib al-Darj: the Chancery of Sultan Barquq

stops.name: Bayn al-Qasrayn, the madrasa-khanqah of Barquq
stops.date_confidence: construction begun December 1384, finished per the facade inscription in April 1386; day not given
stops.campa: The Circassian sultan al-Zahir Barquq raises his funerary madrasa and khanqah on the main thoroughfare of the old Fatimid city, begun in December 1384 and finished, by the inscription on its facade, in April 1386. It is the signature building of the reign that is about to employ al-Qalqashandi, set a few hundred paces from the madrasa where his teacher lectures. Barquq is not buried in it. His daughter Fatima lies there, and his father, whose remains he had brought in.
suggested_refs: The madrasa-khanqah of Sultan al-Zahir Barquq, Bayn al-Qasrayn, completed 1386

stops.name: The Citadel, entry into the Diwan al-Insha
stops.date_confidence: 791 AH per Arabic Wikipedia and Marefa; the Hijri year is attested, the month is not
stops.campa: In 791 of the Hijra he enters the Diwan al-Insha, the chancery of correspondence, in the Citadel on the Muqattam spur, and takes the post of katib al-darj, Scribe of the Scroll. The work is the drafting of the sultan's letters, treaties, appointments and decrees in the layered rhetorical Arabic the office demands, on paper of prescribed dimensions, with a prescribed form of address for every rank in the known world. He is about thirty-four. Which rooms of the fortress the Diwan occupied is not specified by any source consulted.
stops.quote: became a Scribe of the Scroll (Katib al-Darj), or clerk of the Mamluk chancery in Cairo, Egypt
suggested_refs: The Diwan al-Insha of the Cairo Citadel; the office of katib al-darj

stops.name: Bab Zuwayla and the Qasaba, the scribes' corridor
stops.date_confidence: context rather than event; no document places al-Qalqashandi at any address along this route
stops.campa: For three decades his life runs along the corridor between the Citadel gate and the old Fatimid city, up the Qasaba past the sugar merchants and the paper sellers to the twin minarets standing over Bab Zuwayla. This is the quarter the scribal class lives in, buys its reeds and its ink in, and walks to work through. The corridor is the spine of Mamluk Cairo, and a clerk going up to the fortress has no other way to take. No document places him at any particular door on it.
suggested_refs: Bab Zuwayla and the Qasaba, administrative and commercial spine of Mamluk Cairo
sources: General knowledge of Mamluk Cairo urban geography

stops.name: Cairo, the two years as deputy
stops.date_confidence: no dates given by any source; the year here is a placement inside his career and carries no evidential weight. Coordinates are a central-Cairo placeholder, not a building
stops.campa: One Arabic account gives him a post of two years as na'ib, a deputy, distinct from his scribal work. What kind of deputy is not agreed. Read as na'ib al-hukm the post is a deputy judgeship, which fits a man trained in Shafi'i law; read otherwise it becomes a deputy governorship, which fits nothing else known about him. No court is named and no years are given, and the second Arabic encyclopedia consulted does not mention the post at all. Nobody now can say which office it was. A deputy judge in Mamluk Cairo hears the business the chief qadi of his school has no hours for: inheritance, endowments, debt.
suggested_refs: The disputed two-year deputyship: na'ib al-hukm or na'ib of a province

stops.name: The Northern Cemetery, the death of Barquq
stops.date_confidence: attested; 20 June 1399 falls in 801 AH, the year Arabic sources give as the end of al-Qalqashandi's first chancery term
stops.campa: Barquq dies on 20 June 1399, in 801 of the Hijra, and Arabic sources date the end of al-Qalqashandi's first stretch of chancery service to the end of that reign. The sultan had ordered a great khanqah built for himself out in the northern cemetery and set aside eighty thousand dinars for it, but the complex rising on this ground is his son's work, begun after the funeral and finished around 1411. The son, an-Nasir Faraj, is thirteen years old when the sultanate falls to him.
stops.quote: to the end of the reign of al-Zahir Barquq, in the year 801 AH
suggested_refs: The Khanqah of Faraj ibn Barquq in Cairo's Northern Cemetery, built 1400-1411

stops.name: The Citadel, drafting through the wars of Faraj
stops.date_confidence: the reign is attested; the specific month here marks the succession rather than a dated act of al-Qalqashandi's
stops.campa: The reign that follows is broken twice by revolts of the emirs, and Timur's armies take Aleppo and Damascus at the turn of the century. The chancery works through all of it. A state at war has more letters to send than a state at peace: safe-conducts, truces, appointments to governorships that change hands twice in a year. Faraj is deposed and restored inside his own reign, and each turn of it requires its own documents of appointment. Al-Qalqashandi is at his desk for all of it.
suggested_refs: The twice-interrupted reign of an-Nasir Faraj, 1399-1412

stops.name: Cairo, the genealogies of the Arabs
stops.date_confidence: undated. No source consulted dates this work; the position here follows the ordering of the works lists only. Coordinates are the city, not a site
stops.campa: Before the encyclopedia he compiles Nihayat al-Arab fi Ma'rifat Ansab al-Arab, on the descent lines of the Arabs, working from the written tradition rather than from informants. Neither the year nor the place within Cairo is recorded, and the position given here follows the ordering of the works lists alone. The chancery is a fitting place for the subject: forms of address depend on lineage, and a secretary who cannot place a tribe cannot write to its chief correctly.
suggested_refs: Nihayat al-Arab fi Ma'rifat Ansab al-Arab

stops.name: Cairo, the tribes of his own time
stops.date_confidence: undated; sources place it before or during the encyclopedia's composition and give no year
stops.campa: A second genealogical book follows, Qala'id al-Juman fi al-Ta'rif bi-Qaba'il Arab al-Zaman, on the Arab tribes of his own day rather than of the ancestral past. No year of composition survives, and no place within Cairo either. The distinction is a working one for a chancery: the tribes of the present are the ones that can be written to, taxed, garrisoned or paid, and their shaykhs are the ones whose titles have to be got right at the first attempt, in a letter that will be read aloud in a tent somewhere south of Gaza.
suggested_refs: Qala'id al-Juman fi al-Ta'rif bi-Qaba'il Arab al-Zaman

stops.name: The Citadel, Subh al-a'sha begun
stops.date_confidence: 805 AH per Arabic Wikipedia and Marefa; the Hijri year straddles 1402 and 1403 and no month is recorded
stops.campa: In 805 of the Hijra he begins the book that will swallow the next ten years: Subh al-a'sha fi Sina'at al-Insha, the Dawn of the Blind on the Craft of Chancery Composition. The title is a courtesy toward its readers, night-blind clerks groping for a form of words at a desk. He works from the Diwan's own archive of state correspondence, from the administrative compilations of Shihab al-Din al-Umari, and from the geographers, assembling a reference that will let a secretary draft anything the sultanate can require.
stops.quote: His magnum opus is the voluminous administrative encyclopedia Ṣubḥ al-Aʿshá
suggested_refs: Subh al-a'sha fi Sina'at al-Insha, begun 805 AH; al-Umari's Masalik al-absar as a principal source

stops.name: The Citadel, the world described from a desk
stops.date_confidence: the geographical volumes belong to the 805-814 AH composition span; the year is a marker within it
stops.campa: The geographical volumes run from al-Andalus to China: provinces, rivers, road distances, the postal relays and the pigeon towers that carry a sultan's order from Cairo to Damascus in a matter of days. He compiles them from the earlier geographers and from the diplomatic files on his own shelves, in a fortress above one city. No source consulted attests that he traveled beyond Egypt, and that absence is a silence in the record rather than a proven negative.
suggested_refs: The geographical books of Subh al-a'sha, from al-Andalus to China

stops.name: Jerusalem, the mosaics on the al-Aqsa walls
stops.date_confidence: his account is dated only to the early fifteenth century. No source consulted attests a journey to Jerusalem; the coordinates are the mosque, not an attested stop on his itinerary
stops.campa: Writing in the early fifteenth century, he describes the mosaic decoration on the walls of the al-Aqsa Mosque, and that description is still cited as evidence for the building's fabric. Whether he saw the mosaics with his own eyes is stated by no source consulted, and these coordinates are the mosque rather than an attested stop on any journey of his. He is a Cairo secretary compiling a manual for clerks, and the paragraph on the mosaics sits inside it among the forms of address.
suggested_refs: Al-Qalqashandi's early fifteenth-century account of the al-Aqsa mosaics

stops.name: The Citadel, the chapter on ciphers
stops.date_confidence: the cipher section belongs to the completed work of 814 AH; no separate date of drafting is recorded
stops.campa: Among the treatises there is a section on ciphers, and it is the reason the book is read outside the study of Mamluk administration. It sets out substitution and transposition, gives tables of letter frequency, lists the pairs of letters that cannot stand together in an Arabic word, and describes assigning several symbols to one plaintext letter so that the counting fails. The material is Ibn al-Durayhim's, quoted. The ninety-character threshold buried inside it is Ibn Adlan's, and Ibn Adlan is not named.
stops.quote: Kahn therefore cited it as the first work in human history that described cryptology, because it described both cryptography and cryptanalysis
stops.quote_source: Wikipedia, 'Al-Qalqashandi', citing David Kahn, The Codebreakers
suggested_refs: The cryptology section of Subh al-a'sha; David Kahn, The Codebreakers

stops.name: Cairo, an introduction and ten treatises
stops.date_confidence: the structure is described as of the work's completion in Shawwal 814 AH
stops.campa: The finished work is an introduction and ten treatises: the qualifications and the ethics required of a secretary, the geography of the Islamic lands with Egypt at the centre, the forms and protocols of official correspondence and decree, the ranks and honorifics of kings and judges and scholars, models of Mamluk documents, the classification of governorships, the drafting of oaths and treaties and safe-conducts, sample royal letters, and the history of the postal system down to the carrier pigeons. The whole runs to fourteen volumes in the modern editions.
stops.quote: Ṣubḥ al-Aʿshá fī Ṣināʿat al-Inshāʾ ('The Dawn of the Blind' or 'Daybreak for the Night-Blind regarding the Composition of Chancery Documents'); a fourteen-volume encyclopedia completed in 1412, is an administrative manual on geography, political history, natural history, zoology, mineralogy, cosmography, and time measurement
suggested_refs: The ten maqalat of Subh al-a'sha and its muqaddima

stops.name: Cairo, finished in Shawwal
stops.date_confidence: Shawwal 814 AH, which falls in the opening months of 1412; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: He finishes in Shawwal of 814, the first months of 1412 by the Christian reckoning, ten years after beginning. Arabic and English sources agree on the date, and not one of them records who the completed work was dedicated to: Faraj, who is weeks from being killed, the caliph al-Musta'in, who will be installed as a stopgap, or al-Mu'ayyad Shaykh, who takes the throne later in the same year. A chancery manual of this size is normally presented to a sovereign with a preface naming him. Who was this one handed to? The record does not say.
stops.quote: one of the final expressions of the genre of Arabic administrative literature
suggested_refs: The completion of Subh al-a'sha, Shawwal 814 AH; the unresolved question of its dedicatee

stops.name: The Citadel, the news from Damascus
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: Faraj is stabbed in his cell at Damascus on 23 May 1412
stops.campa: Months after the encyclopedia is finished, the sultan under whom it was written loses his army to the Syrian emirs at Baalbek, flees into the citadel of Damascus, and surrenders. On 23 May 1412 a hired assassin stabs him to death in his prison cell there. He is twenty-six, and had held the throne, with one interruption, since the age of thirteen. The emirs raise the Abbasid caliph al-Musta'in Billah in his place as a temporary measure. In Cairo the chancery goes on drafting.
suggested_refs: The deposition and killing of an-Nasir Faraj at Damascus, 23 May 1412

segments.name: Last Works, and a Grave No Source Names

stops.name: Cairo, the caliphate and the law
stops.date_confidence: undated. Neither Arabic Wikipedia nor Marefa dates any of the later works; the year is ordering, not evidence
stops.campa: He goes on writing. Ma'athir al-Inafa fi Ma'alim al-Khilafa treats the history and the offices of the caliphate, the institution the Cairo Abbasids still embodied in ceremony while the Mamluk sultans held everything else. A treatise on Shafi'i jurisprudence, al-Ghiyuth al-Hawami', comes from the same stretch of years, the only sign that the law he trained in stayed with him after the chancery took his working hours. No source dates either book, describes the circumstances of its writing, or says whether it was ever copied twice.
suggested_refs: Ma'athir al-Inafa fi Ma'alim al-Khilafa; al-Ghiyuth al-Hawami' fi al-Fiqh

stops.name: Cairo, the encyclopedia cut down to size
stops.date_confidence: undated; placed after 814 AH on the sources' own ordering
stops.campa: He abridges his own encyclopedia into Daw' al-Subh al-Musfir wa Ghunyat al-Mustafid wa'l-Musafir, a portable Dawn for the user and the traveler, fourteen volumes cut to something a working secretary could carry on a journey. A second abridgement, Janna al-Dawh al-Muthmir, is named in some listings and is absent from the Arabic works list retrieved for this account. Neither abridgement carries a date, and no copy of the second is placed in any library by the sources consulted.
suggested_refs: Daw' al-Subh al-Musfir wa Ghunyat al-Mustafid wa'l-Musafir, the author's own abridgement

stops.name: Cairo, out of office and in standing
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from a single Arabic biographical page; the year is a marker in his final period and no source gives one
stops.campa: In his last years he leaves active chancery office and keeps his rank at the court, living in relative seclusion. One source says so, and nothing else consulted either confirms it or contradicts it. What the seclusion contained, whether teaching, copying, dictation to a son, or nothing at all, the record does not say. He is past sixty, and no source consulted names a student of his, a house he lived in, or a manuscript in his own hand. The sultanate he drafted for changed hands twice in 1412 alone.
suggested_refs: The reported retirement of al-Qalqashandi from chancery office, single-source

stops.name: Cairo, the sixteenth of July
stops.date_confidence: attested: 821 AH, given as 16 July 1418 CE by Arabic Wikipedia and confirmed as 1418 by Marefa and English Wikipedia
stops.campa: Ahmad al-Qalqashandi dies at Cairo on 16 July 1418, in 821 of the Hijra. English sources give his age as sixty-two or sixty-three and Arabic sources as about sixty-five, and the two figures are one lifetime counted twice: 821 less 756 is sixty-five lunar years, which comes to roughly sixty-three solar ones. It is an artifact of two calendars and not a disagreement about the year he was born. Of the death itself nothing is described: no illness, no deathbed, no witness, no funeral.
stops.quote: a medieval Arab Egyptian encyclopedist, polymath and mathematician
suggested_refs: The death of al-Qalqashandi, 821 AH / 16 July 1418, at Cairo

stops.name: Cairo, a burial nobody records
stops.date_confidence: the burial is undated and unlocated; the date here is the day after death by custom, and the coordinates are the city
stops.campa: No tomb, mosque or cemetery is named for him in the English or the Arabic encyclopedia or in Marefa. All three simply stop at the date of death. For a Mamluk scholar of his standing this is unusual, since the Qarafa cemeteries south and east of the city hold the documented, visited, catalogued graves of hundreds of his contemporaries. His is not among them, or is not identified among them. The man who wrote the definitive description of Mamluk protocol, including the protocol of funerals and of the titles cut into tombstones, leaves no stone anyone has found.
suggested_refs: The unrecorded burial place of al-Qalqashandi; the Qarafa cemeteries of Cairo
sources: Gap noted across Wikipedia, Arabic Wikipedia and Marefa entries on al-Qalqashandi

stops.name: Bulaq, the encyclopedia into type
stops.date_confidence: 1323 AH per Arabic Wikipedia; the Hijri year corresponds to 1905 and no month is given
stops.campa: Four hundred and ninety-one years after it was finished, and nearly four centuries after the Ottomans ended the sultanate it was written for, the Bulaq press in Cairo sets part of Subh al-a'sha in type. Until then the fourteen volumes had lived where they were meant to live, in manuscript, copied by clerks for the use of other clerks. The edition is partial. Arabic Wikipedia gives its year as 1323 of the Hijra and does not say which volumes went to the press or how many copies were run.
suggested_refs: The Bulaq Press partial edition of Subh al-a'sha, 1323 AH / 1905

stops.name: Oxford, three volumes of a planned seven
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the zincograph printing covered three of a planned seven volumes and was never completed
stops.campa: A lithographic printing appears at Oxford in 1913, three volumes of a projected seven, and stops there. European orientalists had been quarrying the encyclopedia for decades already. Ferdinand Wustenfeld published a partial German translation in 1879, and two Arabists put its correspondence sections into French, Henri Sauvaire and the Belgian Jesuit Henri Lammens. Which of the two took the royal diplomatic letters and which the general Arabic correspondence is given one way in the Arabic account and the other way round in the English.
suggested_refs: The 1913 Oxford zincograph printing; Wustenfeld's 1879 partial German translation

stops.name: Cairo, the complete fourteen volumes
stops.date_confidence: issued between 1331 and 1338 AH, 1913 to 1920 CE; the start year is used as the pin
stops.campa: The Egyptian National Library issues the first complete fourteen-volume edition at Cairo between 1331 and 1338 of the Hijra, 1913 to 1920 in the Christian count. Five centuries after Shawwal 814 the whole book is in print, in the city it describes, produced by the state library of a country then under British occupation. It becomes the standard reference for Mamluk chancery practice: protocol, titulature, postal routes, the wording of an oath or a truce.

stops.name: Beirut, the edition everyone cites
stops.date_confidence: 1409 AH per Arabic Wikipedia, corresponding to 1987
stops.campa: Dar al-Kutub al-Ilmiyya of Beirut brings out the reprint that most later scholarship cites, edited by Muhammad Husayn Shams al-Din, in 1409 of the Hijra. By now the encyclopedia is consulted for every purpose except the one it was written for; nobody drafts a Mamluk safe-conduct out of it. Historians of Egypt, of diplomacy, of the postal relay, of Jerusalem's mosaics and of cryptology work from the same fourteen volumes. The Beirut text is the one their footnotes point to.

stops.name: Cryptologia, April 1992: the chain made legible
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month of publication. The pin is Cairo, the city the chain runs through; the paper itself belongs to no place on this map
stops.campa: The journal Cryptologia publishes Ibrahim al-Kadi's paper on the origins of cryptology and the Arab contribution, and in English the chain becomes legible: al-Kindi in ninth-century Baghdad, Ibn Adlan at the Salihiyya, Ibn al-Durayhim and his eight systems, and al-Qalqashandi copying the whole of it into a manual for clerks. The histories in English had until then credited the European Renaissance with inventing the discipline. David Kahn had already put the case at its bluntest.
stops.quote: Cryptology was born among the Arabs
stops.quote_source: David Kahn, quoted in Muslim Heritage, 'Arab Origins of Cryptology'

stops.name: Cairo, the treatise that may or may not survive
stops.date_confidence: no source consulted dates the reported rediscovery; the date is set just after the April 1992 paper for ordering only and carries no evidential weight
stops.campa: Whether Ibn al-Durayhim's own treatise survives is the point at which the sources stop agreeing. One account holds that it was once considered lost and is known through al-Qalqashandi's quotation of it. The article on Ibn al-Durayhim himself says the manuscript was recently discovered and has yet to be published. A third states flatly that his writings on cryptography have been lost. No source consulted places the manuscript in a named library, and the famous Istanbul rediscovery belongs to a different text, by al-Kindi.
stops.quote: This information was attributed to Ibn al-Durayhim who lived from AD 1312 to 1361, but whose writings on cryptography have been lost

stops.name: Cairo, the encyclopedia re-edited
stops.date_confidence: the 2017 selections are attested; their form is disputed, being cited as a journal article and described elsewhere as a Routledge monograph in the Al-Masaq series
stops.campa: Scholarly re-editing goes on. In 1972 the International Journal of Middle East Studies carried two articles on what the encyclopedia records of the hierarchy, titles and appointment of Christian and Jewish religious dignitaries in Mamluk Egypt and Syria. In 2017 Heba el-Toudy and Tarek Galal Abdelhamid published selections on the seats of government and the regulations of the kingdom under the Al-Masaq imprint, cited in one place as a journal article and described in another as a book in a series. Which of the two it is has not been settled.
suggested_refs: El-Toudy and Abdelhamid, Selections from Subh al-A'sha (Al-Masaq, 2017); IJMES 3:1 and 3:2 (1972)
